tables.context_before:
Patient Population
This CPG addresses the management of falls and fall
risk in community-dwelling older adults. It is not
intended to address the management of falls and fall
risk in older adults who are institutionalized. Those
who are institutionalized may be at a greater risk of
falls but require care specific to the acute condition,
nursing home facility, or change in cognition, to name
a few examples. This CPG specifically defines community-dwelling older adults as 65 or over who do not
have major health conditions that prevent them from
interacting in their environment without substantia
tables.text:
Recommendation | Level of Evidence | Strength of Recommendation
Physical therapists should participate in multifactoriala management programs addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponentb exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate of falls and it must include balance training and may include other exercise modes. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to 3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and must include progressive and sufficiently challenging balance training. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe balance training to older adults that is progressive and sufficiently challenging as evidenced by movement of the limbs and whole body in multiple directions, changing the base of support, and reducing upper limb support either alone or as part of a multicomponent program to reduce the risk and rate of falls. | I | Strong
Balance training must include volitional step training and/or gait adaptability training. | I | Strong
Balance training may also include reactive step (perturbation) training. | II | Weak
Physical therapists should NOT provide or prescribe resistance training ALONE to older adults if the purpose is to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls. | II | Moderate
Physical therapists should prescribe Tai Chi for older adults to reduce the risk and rate of falls. | I | Strong
Physical therapists should NOT provide education ALONE to older adults to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls. | I | Strong
Physical therapists should provide tailored education combined with individualized exercise intervention to older adults. The tailored education should include specific actions to address identified risk factors, including home hazards and strength and balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT scope of practice. | V | Expert opinion
Physical therapists should provide environmental assessment and recommend modifications to older adults at high risk of falls. | I | Strong
aMultifactorial management includes screening, assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice. bMulticomponent exercise refers to exercise that includes more than one category of exercise according to the PROFANE1 taxonomy (balance and functional, flexibility, resistance training, 3-D). |  |
rows: Physical therapists should participate in multifactoriala management programs addressing falls and fall risk for older adults.
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponentb exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate of falls and it must include balance training and may include other exercise modes.

Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to 3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and must include progressive and sufficiently challenging balance training.

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe balance training to older adults that is progressive and sufficiently challenging as evidenced by movement of the limbs and whole body in multiple directions, changing the base of support, and reducing upper limb support either alone or as part of a multicomponent program to reduce the risk and rate of falls.
Balance training must include volitional step training and/or gait adaptability training.
Balance training may also include reactive step (perturbation) training.
Physical therapists should NOT provide or prescribe resistance training ALONE to older adults if the purpose is to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls.
Physical therapists should prescribe Tai Chi for older adults to reduce the risk and rate of falls.
Physical therapists should NOT provide education ALONE to older adults to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls.

Physical therapists should provide tailored education combined with individualized exercise intervention to older adults. The tailored education should include specific actions to address identified risk factors, including home hazards and strength and balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT scope of practice.
Physical therapists should provide environmental assessment and recommend modifications to older adults at high risk of falls.

aMultifactorial management includes screening, assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice. bMulticomponent exercise refers to exercise that includes more than one category of exercise according to the PROFANE1 taxonomy (balance and functional, flexibility, resistance training, 3-D).

RESULTS
The search strategies are provided in Supplemental Digital
Content, Appendix I (available at: http://links.lww.com/
JGPT/A267). The initial search was conducted in 2015,
with updates in 2018 and 2022. Therefore, the final search
results included studies from 2005 through 2022. In total
1549 articles were identified and 55 were included. See
Figure 2 and Supplemental Digital Content, Appendix II

Screening
Physical therapists’ management of falls is predicated on
their ability to identify fall risk and movement dysfunction
as part of a multifactorial evaluation process to guide treatment choice. In 2017, through the Geriatrics Evidence
Database to Guide Effectiveness Initiative (GeriEDGE) task
force, Lusardi et al published a systematic review of history
questions, self-report measures, and performance-based
measures for assessing fall risk of community-dwelling
older adults.13 This CPG developed a screening process
using these results13 and the previous guidance statement
recommendati

 | Falls Efficacy Scale – International | >24 points

Multicomponent exercise interventions provided by
a health professional and by a trained instructor who is
not a health professional are effective in reducing falls
rate.28 The GDG valued having a health professional
trained in exercise prescription to monitor and progress
multicomponent exercise programs. The GDG judged this
to be particularly important in populations with movement dysfunction or health conditions that may impact
the ability to exercise. Older adults with lower fall risk
who are safe to exercise alone may benefit equally from
a physical therapist delivering a tailored interve
